newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn coalition, SPD face drawn-out reform battle.
newsitem.headline: Bonn coalition, SPD face drawn-out reform battle.

text.p: German politicians face a long struggle over reforms to the creaking tax and welfare systems after cross-party talks failed to reach an early deal on tax cuts, analysts said on Wednesday.
High unemployment and the need to cut borrowing to qualify for Europe's single currency had driven Chancellor Helmut Kohl and opposition Social Democrats (SPD) to the negotiating table.
But after three sessions in as many months, the talks broke up in acrimony after finding little common ground on Finance Minister Theo Waigel's plan to slash 30 billion marks ($18 billion) in tax.
Now the focus moves to parliament, where Kohl faces another confrontation with the SPD which could badly hurt both sides if it drags on into the autumn 1998 general election campaign.
"The quicker the tax issue gets into parliament, the quicker it should come to a deal," said analyst Hans-Joachim Veen of the conservative-leaning Konrad Adenauer Foundation.
"Neither of the two big parties can afford to let the tax reforms drag on for the next 18 months," Veen told Reuters.
Lacking a majority in parliament's Bundesrat upper house, Kohl does not have the power to ram through the type of market reforms which have boosted Britain's economic competitiveness.

In the face of bitter SPD and trade union opposition, he has also been unable to construct the kind of broad consensus which enabled the Netherlands to halve unemployment with the help of ambitious labour market reforms.

And Germany's system of fixed parliaments virtually rules out calling snap elections -- as French President Jacques Chirac has done -- to settle the debate on how much pain voters will accept for the sake of European monetary union (EMU).
Pundits have begun asking whether that might not be a better system, but politicians here reject this.

"It would not be good if, 18 months before the general election, we got so badly caught up in campaigning that we lose the capacity for sensible political debate," Saxony state premier Kurt Biedenkopf said.
"Then we would always have to bring elections forward," he told German radio.

Waigel expects his 1998 and 1999 tax bills to clear the lower house of parliament before the summer recess. The measures will then be bounced back by the Bundesrat into parliament's mediation committee for review during the summer.
Then, the horse-trading will resume until a tax compromise acceptable to both sides is hammered out.
Parallel to Germany's slow-moving legislative procedure, Kohl is also hoping to force the SPD into cracking on tax under pressure from German voters.

Peter Hintze, general secretary of Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), fired a first pre-election salvo by saying the tax debate would be fought out on the campaign trail in state elections leading up to next year's national vote.

"The voters in Hamburg, Lower Saxony and Saxony-Anhalt have the power to break the SPD blockade in the forthcoming state elections," Hintze said in a statement. All three are SPD-led and form part of the opposition majority in the Bundesrat.

Analysts have attributed the hostility of the SPD to the government tax reforms to an internal struggle between leader Oskar Lafontaine and challenger-in-waiting Lower Saxony premier Gerhard Schroeder -- who is more doveish on tax.

With both sides standing pat on reforms and the two main parties both having to face down internal critics, economists worry that Bonn will not be able to do what is necessary to meet EMU's stringent borrowing targets this year.

Only on Tuesday, Germany's authoritative six economic research institutes had warned that uncertainties arising from delays to fiscal reforms could damage the country's bid to cut borrowing below the EMU goal of three percent of GDP.
"Getting rid of these uncertainties alone would have positive impact," the institutes said their half-yearly report.
Financial analysts warned that Waigel's tax reforms could be watered down in parliament, and political uncertainty in the meantime would dampen investment and growth.

"The government will continue to try to push this through the legislative process, but the chances are very slim indeed that the reform will come through as it stands," said Holger Fahrinkrug, economist at UBS in Frankfurt. ($ = 1.713 German Marks)
